title: Pride Brought Down
sum: Obadiah is the shortest book of the Old Testament: one chapter, twenty-one verses, one main target. Edom, the nation descended from Jacob's twin brother Esau, is told it will be brought down from its cliff-top strongholds (verses 1-9). The reason comes in verses 10-14. When foreigners took Jerusalem, Edom stood aside, gloated, helped itself to the loot and cut off the refugees. Eight times the LORD says "do not" to something Edom did on "the day" of its brother's disaster.

Then the book turns (verse 15). The day of the LORD is near for all the nations, and what Edom did will come back on its own head. The last six verses promise Zion survivors, a Jacob that burns like fire against an Esau that is only stubble, a wide map of recovered lands, and rescuers on Mount Zion. They end on the book's real subject: "royal power will belong to the LORD." Verses 1-9 closely resemble Jeremiah 49:7-22, and how the two are related is one of the book's main puzzles.
readings: A word from the days after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, spoken for the survivors: a neighbor and kinsman helped the destroyers, and the LORD saw it. The book gives the wounded a reason to believe the wrong has been noticed.

Edom stands for any proud, secure power that profits from a neighbor's disaster. "As you did, it will be done to you" is stated as a rule for all the nations (verse 15). The cliff-top boast (verses 3-4) is the pattern of pride everywhere.
Read as a hope for the scattered
The last verses speak to exiles in Zarephath and Sepharad: the lost lands will be taken back and the LORD will reign. For people with no land and no king, the closing line names who has the power.

views.H: The commonest dating puts verses 10-14 soon after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 25:12-14; Ezekiel 35; Jeremiah 40:11; Malachi 1:2-5). An older view looks to the 800s BC, when Edom revolted under Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 21:8-17), or to Ahaz's day (2 Chronicles 28:17). Edom's kingdom faded under Arab and then Nabataean pressure, and the Edomites settled as Idumeans in southern Judea (1 Maccabees 5:3, 65; Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1).
views.C: The main questions are the link between verses 1-9 and Jeremiah 49:7-22 (borrowing either way, or a common source), the unity of the book (verses 1-14, about Edom; verses 15-21, about the day of the LORD and Zion, perhaps added later, since Gilead, Zarephath and Sepharad point to a scattered Judah), and the book's place in the Twelve (it follows Amos 9:12, "the remnant of Edom," and Joel's day of the LORD). The scrolls 4QXIIg and Mur 88 agree with the Masoretic Text almost throughout.
views.J: Edom is Esau, and rabbinic literature from the Talmudic period on often reads Esau and Edom as Rome. The Targum reads Sepharad as Spain; the equation of Zarephath with France is in the Talmud (Bavli Yoma 10a) and was followed by medieval commentators, which is why Sepharad and Tsarfat became names for medieval Jewish communities. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 39b) is reported to call Obadiah an Edomite convert. In Sephardic custom Obadiah is the prophetic reading (haftarah) for Vayishlach, the week in which Jacob meets Esau, and verse 21 is among the kingship verses of the New Year liturgy.
views.X: Church readers have often applied Edom to the enemies of God's people and Zion to the church, with the "rescuers" as the apostles or Christ himself (a later reading, not the author's). Herod the Great was an Idumean, but Obadiah does not predict him. Warning: the Esau/Edom label was sometimes turned against Jews in Christian preaching, a use this site notes and does not follow (see the topic on anti-Judaism).
views.F: Verse 15's day of the LORD "against all the nations," the return of exiles (verses 17-20) and royal power belonging to the LORD (verse 21) are read as still to come. Dispensationalist readers expect a literal restoration in the land. Catholic, Orthodox and many Reformed readers see the promise fulfilled in Christ and the church while still awaiting the final kingdom; Catholic teaching also looks to Israel's full inclusion (Catechism 674), and some Reformed readers expect a future turning of the Jewish people (Romans 11). Many Jewish readers keep the hope of return and the LORD's kingdom.

deep.b:
Obadiah 1-9 and Jeremiah 49:7-22 share material, but the wording differs in most lines. The Plain English Translation translates each from its own Hebrew and matches only where the Hebrew matches.

ObadiahJeremiahWhat differs in the Hebrew
149:14Obadiah: "we have heard" and a call to rise up against "her"; Jeremiah: "I have heard," "gather together and come against her." Obadiah adds "The Lord GOD says this about Edom."
249:15Almost the same. Obadiah ends "greatly despised"; Jeremiah ends "despised among people."
3-449:16Shared in the Hebrew: "the pride of your heart has fooled you" (the Plain English Translation says it the same way in both), "the cracks of the cliff" and "from there I will bring you down." Jeremiah adds "the terror you cause" and "who hold the height of the hill." Obadiah alone has the boast "Who will lower me to the ground?" and the nest among the stars.
549:9Order reversed (Obadiah has the thieves first). Obadiah adds "how ruined you are!" and says the thieves "steal"; Jeremiah says they "ruin."
649:10Jeremiah: the LORD says "I have stripped Esau bare." Obadiah: a cry in the passive, "How Esau has been searched through!"
7noneThe betrayal by allies has no parallel in Jeremiah.
849:7The same idea (wise men of Edom lost) in different words: Jeremiah has "counsel" lost from Teman; Obadiah has the wise destroyed from Edom and "understanding" from Mount Esau.
949:22 (compare 49:20)No shared wording. Both show Edom's warriors breaking: in Jeremiah as a woman in labor, in Obadiah as shattered with fear.
10-14noneEdom's crime against its brother appears only in Obadiah.
1649:12Both use the cup of judgment, with different lines.

Three explanations are given. (1) Obadiah used Jeremiah. (2) Jeremiah used Obadiah, or a form of it. (3) Both used an older oracle or a common stock of sayings about Edom. The order of the lines is not the same, and neither text is simply a copy; the dating of Obadiah's verses 10-14 to after 586 BC makes (3) or (1) more natural to many scholars, while others favor (2). Raabe's commentary and Ben Zvi's study set out the options in detail.

The eight lines of verses 12-14 all begin with the Hebrew 'al ("do not") and a verb:

VerseHebrewPlain English Translation
12aוְאַל־תֵּרֶאDo not look on with delight
12bוְאַל־תִּשְׂמַחDo not be glad
12cוְאַל־תַּגְדֵּל פִּיךָDo not talk big
13aאַל־תָּבוֹאDo not enter my people's gate
13bאַל־תֵּרֶאDo not look with delight
13cוְאַל־תִּשְׁלַחְנָהDo not reach out a hand for their wealth
14aוְאַל־תַּעֲמֹדDo not stand at the crossroads
14bוְאַל־תַּסְגֵּרDo not hand over those who are left

The first three are about attitude and speech (gloating, rejoicing, boasting); the next three about entering and taking; the last two about cutting off escape. The sequence moves from the eyes and mouth to the hands and feet. Each line is tied to "on the day of" the people's trouble, which comes ten times in verses 11-14.

Edom was a kingdom of the high land south and east of the Dead Sea, with its capital at Bozrah (Buseirah). Israel traced its people to Esau, Jacob's twin (Genesis 25-36), and the two nations were bound by kinship and trouble together. David conquered Edom (2 Samuel 8:13-14), Edom revolted under Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20-22), and in the 700s and 600s BC it was a vassal of Assyria and later Babylon. Excavations at Buseirah, Tawilan and Umm el-Biyara show settled towns and fortresses before about 550 BC. After that Arab tribes moved in, Edomites shifted west into the Negev and southern Judea (Idumea), and the Nabataeans built their capital at Petra. John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea about 125 BC and forced the Idumeans to be circumcised. Herod the Great was of Idumean descent. On the commonest dating, Obadiah deals with the Edom of the 500s.
deep.refs: Genesis 25:25-30; Genesis 36:1-8; Numbers 20:14-21; Deuteronomy 23:7; 2 Samuel 8:13-14; 2 Kings 8:20-22; Malachi 1:2-5

deep.title: Ten days, then one day
deep.b: My own observation. The Hebrew word for "day" (yom) comes ten times in verses 11-14, each time for the day Jerusalem fell ("on the day you stood aside," "on the day of his misfortune," "on the day of their calamity"). Then verse 15 says one thing: "the day of the LORD is near." I suggest the repetition is a built-in contrast: the many days of Edom's gloating on the day of Jerusalem's shame are answered by the one day of the LORD. The repeating of "day" is widely noticed; the count of ten and the idea of ten answered by one are my own, and I would not rest anything on the number ten itself.

echoes: Jeremiah 49:7-22; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 25:12-14; Ezekiel 35; Joel 3:3-4, 19; Amos 1:11-12; Amos 9:12; Malachi 1:2-5; Genesis 25-36; Numbers 20:14-21; Deuteronomy 23:7; Isaiah 34:5-17; Isaiah 14:12-15; Isaiah 10:17; Habakkuk 2:8, 16; 1 Maccabees 5:3, 65

settings.by: The LORD, as reported by Obadiah ("we have heard a report from the LORD")
settings.to: Edom is addressed as "you," but the words were spoken or written for Judah. The first hearers were the people of Judah who survived the fall of Jerusalem, in the land or in exile
settings.when: Most likely after 586 BC, when Edom's part in Jerusalem's fall was fresh; an older view puts it in the 800s BC
settings.why: To tell the wounded that Edom's pride and betrayal were seen, and to show that no cliff or ally can protect a nation from the LORD. It gives Judah no sword; it hands the matter to the LORD. Knowing the hearers explains the tone: this is a message of comfort for the victims, not a threat delivered to Edom.
settings.readers: Judeans of the Persian period reading it as part of the Twelve, after Edom's power had faded, could take it as a sign that the LORD's word on Edom had come true.
views: The commonest view. Verses 10-14 look back on the day Babylon took the city, with the same charge as Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 25 and 35.
An older view: the raid on Jerusalem under Jehoram, when Edom revolted (2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 21:16-17). The language of captives, gates and lots suggests a larger event.
Some see verses 1-14 as built from older material and updated in the Persian period, along with the later verses.

settings.to: Edom, as the one accused, and Judah, who overhear the charge
settings.when: Looking back on (or, for some, standing in) "the day" Jerusalem was taken
settings.why: To name the crime and its reason: not that Edom fought, but that a brother stood aside, gloated and helped. Brotherhood raised the duty. Knowing that the eight "do nots" can be warnings or rebukes of what already happened (see the note at verse 12) changes the sense: either a speaker standing at the city's wall, or a verdict after the fact.
settings.readers: Later readers received a standard of kindness toward a neighbor in disaster that applies to every nation.
views: The "do nots" are commands, as if the prophet stood on the day itself.
The "do nots" mean "you should not have"; the day is already past.

settings.what: The day of the LORD and Zion's restoration
settings.by: The LORD, as reported by Obadiah
settings.to: The survivors and exiles of Judah and the northern tribes: Jacob and Joseph, and exiles as far away as Zarephath and Sepharad
settings.when: After 586 BC; many scholars think verses 15b-21 were added or reworked in the Persian period, when Judah was small and many Jews lived abroad
settings.why: To give people with no land, no king and few survivors a reason to hope: the LORD will repay the nations, Zion will have survivors and be holy, and the lost lands will be taken back. The book ends with the LORD's rule, so the hope rests on God and not on Judah's strength.
settings.readers: For Jews who read it in the Twelve, the closing verses joined Amos 9:12 and Joel 3:17-21 in a single promise about Zion and the nations.
views: The lists of lands and the exiles of Jerusalem and Sepharad look to the Babylonian or Persian period.
Some see verses 15b-21 as a Zion-centered supplement to an oracle against Edom.

traditions.q: Who are "the house of Jacob" and "Mount Zion" in verses 17-21, and does the promise of land still hold?
views: The promise is to the Jewish people as a nation, in their land. Classical dispensationalists (Darby, Scofield) keep Israel and the church distinct and expect a literal fulfillment, with the LORD reigning from Zion.

Covenant theology has two streams. One reads the promises to Jacob and Zion as fulfilled in Christ and in the church (Romans 9:6-8). The other also expects a future turning of the Jewish people (Romans 11:25-29), and the Westminster Larger Catechism (question 191) has the church pray for the calling of the Jews. Both treat the end of the book as pointing to the kingdom of Christ.

The Church is the new people of God (Lumen Gentium 9), and the Jews remain dear to God, since God's gifts and call are irrevocable (Nostra Aetate 4, quoting Romans 11:28-29). The Catechism (674, 840) looks to Israel's full inclusion at the end.

A short summary with no source cited here: Orthodox readers have generally read Zion as the Church and Christ's kingdom, reading the Old Testament through Christ, and the Church has no official teaching of a restored Jewish kingdom in the land.

A short summary with no source cited here: the Jewish people keep their calling, and Jewish believers in Jesus are a sign of the remnant. Many look to a restoration at the Messiah's return; views on the land differ.

No separate teaching on Obadiah. Lutheran readers have generally read Zion through Christ and the church (as in the Catholic and Reformed rows), and differ on how to take Romans 11. No confession is cited here.
Baptists are divided between the dispensationalist and the covenant readings above. No confession speaks to Obadiah 17-21.

traditions.q: Is Esau, or Edom, only the nation in Obadiah, or also a picture of the church's enemies or of the world?
views: Scripture has a literal sense and spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, anagogical) that rest on it (Catechism 115-119; Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10). On that approach Edom can be read, beyond the nation, as a figure of those who oppose God's people.
The Fathers read the Old Testament with more than one sense, always centered on Christ. Esau and Jacob are figures in the New Testament (Romans 9:13).

The true sense of any Scripture is one, not manifold (Westminster Confession 1.9). On that rule Obadiah is first a word about Edom, and lessons for the church come by comparison with the nation's pride and fall.
The Second London Confession (1.9) repeats the one-sense rule, which points toward reading Edom as the historic nation, with the lessons about pride applying to anyone.
The literal sense is the only sense: Edom is Edom.

traditions.q: "It will be done to you just as you did it" (verse 15): may believers ask for such payback, or only leave it to God?
views: Believers do not repay evil. Vengeance belongs to God (Romans 12:17-21; Matthew 5:38-45), and texts like Obadiah are God's word of justice, not a charter for believers (Dordrecht Confession, article 14, on revenge).
God punishes wrong through the government's sword, and the individual Christian forgives. Luther's two-kingdoms teaching keeps the two apart (Augsburg Confession XVI).
Obadiah shows a moral order God runs in history. The civil ruler bears the sword (Romans 13:4; Westminster Confession 23.1), but private revenge is forbidden (Westminster Larger Catechism 135-136).
Justice, not revenge: punishment aims at justice, safety and correction (Catechism 2266), legitimate defense may be a duty (2308-2309), and each person must forgive (2842-2845).
